1) You should use it after you have built your software. It double checks if the checksum of the files in the pdb file match the ones on disk ("source control"). Since these are generated files (and the demo app anyway), you can ignore them.

2) You should just included your pdb files in the nuget and all should work automatically.

3) Since there is no specific commit specified to the command line, it will automatically use the latest commit on the current branch for you.

I found how to reproduce this behavior: by default, `Caliburn.Micro` set `Window.SizeToContent` to `SizeToContent.WidthAndHeight`. By default, this value is set to `SizeToContent.Manual`.

When you use `SizeToContent.WidthAndHeight`, I suppose the layout manager give the entire screen size as constraints, because the window can grow up.

![big_font_size](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/846026/5243328/49e3b886-7975-11e4-90f7-7ee9f678502a.png)

So I think the SystemsFont.MenuFont\* will be used as the global font settings for all ribbon controls. Furthermore the layout of the ribbon should be dynamically calculated based on the height of formatted text.

While your fixes regarding height restriction might be correct, the direct references to MenuFontSizeKey etc. won't be accepted, as we would have to add this to every control contained in the ribbon if we would follow your path. In fact the Microsoft Ribbon just sets this at the Ribbon level so every control inherits that setting. Please have a look at the generic.xaml contained in the assembly System.Windows.Controls.Ribbon to see where FontSize is used there.

First, don't try to fix the above issue, because I have prepared another Pull Request that will take care of it.

### Motivation

During my work on this suggestion Pull Request, I didn't understand the reason for the following:
![image](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/1153480/6987188/8e5a7d56-da3c-11e4-98b9-3d21243f8294.png)

I tried to optimize it directly by taking rid off all of this and just using a `ContentPresenter` with `HorizontalAlignment="Center"`, to my surprise what I did broke the end result.

What I understood is that everything as it is in the picture is needed to correctly position the header. I believe it is wrong for two things:
- This is not how items are centered in WPF, `HorizontalAlignment="Center"` should do the job.
- Users might get confused when they try to customize the look. I was.

## Solution

The solution I will discuss is up and running just fine, I will push it in a Pull Request right after this #89 is merged.

![image](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/1153480/6988631/3aea0538-da4b-11e4-8542-8bcd5364a5e2.png)

I took rid off the `RibbonTabItem.MeasureOverride` and the **PART_ContentContainer** dependency, they're no longer needed. The idea is to manipulate the `Padding` of the `RibbonTabItem` and the available space.
I mainly refactored the `RibbonTabsContainer` to:
1. Reduce the Padding value during re-size, we start with the value 17 on both the left and right, after this step we end at 5. 12 is for the default indent.
2. After that we start reducing the width of the control, by width I mean the available space reserved for the control.

For contextual tabs, we have three steps in some cases, because some tabs might be extended to accommodate the length of their enclosing Contextual Group, we reduce it during the second step above.

After you take a look at the final implementation, you will notice that what we have now is similar to what was there.

I talked briefly about my solution, it is already up and fully implemented in the [TabsContainerRewrite](https://github.com/abdelkarim/Fluent.Ribbon/tree/TabsContainerRewrite) branch. It is based on the changes in #89 .

You can change the global theme color using the code snippet below (replace #000000 with your theme color). That changes the color of status bars, backstages, etc.

``` xaml
<Color x:Key="{x:Static Fluent:MetroColors.ThemeColorKey}">#000000</Color>
```

To make it apply globally, you have to merge it with the theme you use (Office2013/Generic.xaml in your case). That will look like this (in App.xaml):

``` xaml
<ResourceDictionary.MergedDictionaries>
    <!--Attach Default Fluent Control's Theme-->
    <ResourceDictionary Source="pack://application:,,,/Fluent;Component/Themes/Generic.xaml" />
    <ResourceDictionary Source="pack://application:,,,/Fluent;Component/Themes/Office2013/Generic.xaml" />
    <ResourceDictionary Source="Design.xaml" /> <!-- this contains your changes to the Fluent theme -->
</ResourceDictionary.MergedDictionaries>
```

I don't know if this is the intended way, but it works and I've not seen any side effects.

I think the difference in color is the intended behavior. 
Other applications by Microsoft that use application menus (i.e. explorer in Windows 8.1) use the application menus background color (#F6F7F8) rather than the ribbons background color (#FFFFFF) for that rectangle.
The gray line in the application menu should line up with the border of the tabs in the ribbon bar (it does that in FluentTest and Windows explorer), but the ribbon tabs in your application seem to have no border at all.

To sum this up:
- To change the background of the StatusBar you currently have to modify the RibbonThemeColorBrush. This could be made easier on our side by setting this background on the Style level rather than the inner border or the control.
- Just changing the Background property on the RibbonTabItem wouldn't help much as you got many colors which are used there. Think of states like "Selected", "Hover" etc. those could, of course, all be exposed but there is nothing planned to implement it in that way. If you want to, feel free to open a new issue and discuss the details of such a change.
- To change the foreground: there is a "DefaultFontBrush" which you could change and see how far you can go with that. Duo to the history of this library, on one side, this was needed in the past. I can image that we could eliminate that one mostly. But we have to set some foreground color somewhere (maybe at the ribbon level) and as I don't need it that way (I can live with the current implementation) I won't change it. On the other side we got many different background colors and so we need different foreground colors. An easy way to be able to find foreground colors is to search for "FontBrush" and see which ones you need to change according to your requirements.

To change the color of that rectangle you have to overwrite "RibbonBackgoundBrush" at least in the scope of the ApplicationMenu like so

```
<Fluent:ApplicationMenu.Resources>

</Fluent:ApplicationMenu.Resources>
```

If you know all tabs at compile-time, it is probably the best idea to add them in xaml, because the gain by having a smaller visual tree is probably not worth the additional work. 
It also sounds like you might want to use contextual groups, which allow you to group tabs that are only useful/available in a certain context. That way the user gets a visual clue, that there are additional commands available based on the context. You can also easily hide entire `RibbonContextualTabGroup`s by setting their visibility property.
If you want to handle the `RibbonTabItem`s in the views, you can bind the `Tabs` property of the ribbon to a `ObservableCollection<RibbonTabItem>` which is composed and changed based on the current view in the code behind. You can access wpf resources with `this.Resources["yourKey"]` from the code behind, but if you define the tabs in a central xaml file anyway, you might as well just define them inside the ribbon of the target window (unless of course you will use the tabs in more than one window).

It is not exactly what you (ghostriderace) wanted, but this is as close as I got to a solution:
You can use the following to display a non-interactive image of a visual:

``` xaml
    <Rectangle Width="250" Height="128">
        <Rectangle.Fill>
            <VisualBrush Stretch="Uniform" Visual="{Binding ElementName=YourContent}" />
        </Rectangle.Fill>
    </Rectangle>
```

This works perfectly fine, as long as the rectangle itself isn't part of the visual that should be shown. You can show the main content of your window, but you have to exclude the Ribbon (as that would include the backstage with your preview area). That obviously also means, that you can't use the window itself as source, because that would include the ribbon...

The problem with loading the controls again on application startup is caused by the implementation of QAT state management.
The code is very simple and stupid. It just saves the positions of the items and tries to grab the corresponding items when it's loaded again.
One saved item looks like this "0,3,1,0,0,3,0,0," and nothing more.
So for your dynamically added items you run into the problem that aren't part of the ribbon when the state is loaded.

I would strongly advice you to not used the included method of saving and loading QAT items as you will, most probably, change the positions of your generated or generate them in a different order in the future. The result you'll get then is that you get some "random" controls restored to QAT.

I don't use dynamic QAT and state management at all at work because our ribbon is massively generated at runtime. There is not a single fixed item in our Ribbon.
To be honest, I won't change/improve the current QAT saving and loading because I don't use it at all.

Just to make sure that I get that right: you want to add a button to your ribbon which disables the ribbon when it is clicked and keeps it disabled until you re-enable it programmatically.
If that is the case, you can use a `Fluent:ToggleButton` and its `IsChecked` property. That results in something like that:

```
    <Fluent:RibbonWindow.Resources>
        <Style x:Key="rbnDisabled"
               TargetType="{x:Type Fluent:Ribbon}">
            <Setter Property="IsEnabled"
                    Value="True" />
            <Style.Triggers>
                <DataTrigger Binding="{Binding ElementName=g3b2, Path=IsChecked}"
                             Value="True">
                    <Setter Property="IsEnabled"
                            Value="False"></Setter>
                </DataTrigger>
            </Style.Triggers>
        </Style>
    </Fluent:RibbonWindow.Resources>
    <Grid>
        <Fluent:Ribbon Style="{StaticResource rbnDisabled}">
            <!--Tabs-->
            <Fluent:RibbonTabItem Header="Tab">
                <Fluent:RibbonGroupBox Header="Group">
                    <Fluent:ToggleButton Name="g3b2"
                                   IsChecked="False"
                                   Header="Green" />
                </Fluent:RibbonGroupBox>
            </Fluent:RibbonTabItem>
        </Fluent:Ribbon>
    </Grid>
```

Please note, that this will disable the ribbon and all controls within the ribbon. The `Fluent:ToggleButton` will be disabled (and therefore not clickable anymore) as well as a result, once it is clicked.

I still consider this a bug in WPF, but I found a workaround.

The reason why this issue occurs is because WPF does not find the ancestor of type Fluent:Backstage anymore.
The funny/sad thing is with this code:

```
<Condition Binding="{Binding IsOpen, RelativeSource={RelativeSource AncestorType={x:Type Fluent:Backstage}}}" Value="True" />
<Condition Binding="{Binding IsOpenAnimationEnabled, RelativeSource={RelativeSource AncestorType={x:Type Fluent:Backstage}}}" Value="True" />
```

Guess what happens here...
The first condition throws no binding error. The second one does, because the ancestor could not be found.

I had two usecases in mind.
1. When you have an application with only a few icons that's going to be used on large screens.
2. When you want to have a rectangular shaped icon in your application.

Assume that you have an application that only requires a few buttons and tabs. When having a big screen, the 32x32 icon of the Large button size might not cut it. Specially not when pairing with a single line header.
So instead, I wanted to have the possibility of overruling the iconsize. Having a one-line header, consisting of a key word only, really looks awesome when paired with a 48x48 icon.

Instead of adding another Button type, I went with the IconHeight / IconWidth size, to also allow the possibility of having a differently shaped icon, in the form of 32x48 for example.

I really need this feature in my application so I did some research on touch mode. What i have done here already fits my needs very well but it is not a complete general solution and it is just meant to be discussed as a starting point. 

The following applies to ToggleButton, Button, SplitButton, ColorGallery and DropDownButton only, all used in LargeIcon mode since the other modes are not really useful here to me (I use resistive imprecise monitors on which small controls can't do the job).

## 

In touch mode we need the controls to be more distant from one another or larger.
I started investigating the distance among controls but i immediately understood it was not enough to provide a good user experience. So I investigated custom control sizes also because it is requested in #298.

In Fluent ribbon, controls try to use less space as possible: this feature do not fit in touch mode so the first thing is to provide the possibility to set the Width of a control. This can be achieved very easily this way and in a similar way on most (if not all) controls:

```
<ControlTemplate x:Key="RibbonToggleButtonControlTemplate"
                    TargetType="{x:Type Fluent:ToggleButton}">
    <Border x:Name="border"
            Width="{TemplateBinding Width}" //add this
            MinWidth="{TemplateBinding MinWidth}" //add this
                ...
```

This way all controls can be sized as we wish (can it fix #298?). I size them all to the same size in order to provide a uniform way of interaction.

The current rule to use less space as possible can be achived by setting Width=Auto. So we don't lose that feature.
At the time I switch between TouchMode and normal/mouse mode by the means on a property in my viewmodel (but this should be moved inside Fluent.Ribbon I think) this way:

```
<Style TargetType="{x:Type Fluent:ToggleButton}"  BasedOn="{StaticResource {x:Type Fluent:ToggleButton}}">

Right now I have not that much time but after a bit of debugging I can say this:

In your `Fluent.KeyTipAdorner` there is a method called `UpdateKeyTipPositions()`.

In case of no auto placement this method goes through a couple of possible cases like if the associated element is a `DialogLauncherButton` or if it is within a `RibbonGallery` and so on.

If none of these cases is `true` there is a last condition that checks if the size of the associated element is not `RibbonControlSize.Large` and if the associated element is not a `Spinner`, `ComboBox`, `TextBox` or `CheckBox`. I admit that I did not check this code very thoroughly but the conditions suggest that this case should handle all `KeyTip` placements for controls shaped like a `TextBox`.
The other case seems to handle all controls with a size set to `RibbonControlSize.Large` like a `Button`.

Now because I did not change the size of my `KeyTipedSlider` and because it is neither a `Spinner`, `ComboBox`, `TextBox` or a `CheckBox` it is handled like a button. I have no idea why it works without a button in previous position but I know that setting the `Size` to `RibbonControlSize.Middle` will do the trick.

That's currently by design. Only the GalleryPanel contained in the popup is grouped. If you want immediate grouping you would have to use a GalleryPanel instead of InRibbonGallery.

This code should do what you expect and might also fix 3. and 4.
```
<fluent:ComboBox Grid.Row="1"
                 Grid.Column="0"
                 Header="Select Color"
                 InputWidth="100"
                 Text="{Binding SelectedText, Mode=OneWay}"
                 IsReadOnly="True"
                 HorizontalAlignment="Right"
                 IsManipulationEnabled="True"
                 IsDropDownOpen="{Binding IsDropDownOpen}"
                 IsEditable="True"
                 ItemsSource="{Binding DataItems}"
                 SelectedItem="{Binding SelectedModel}">
    <fluent:ComboBox.ItemsPanel>
        <ItemsPanelTemplate>
            <fluent:GalleryPanel MinItemsInRow="1"
                                 MaxItemsInRow="5"
                                 ItemWidth="50"
                                 ItemHeight="18"
                                 ItemContainerGenerator="{Binding ItemContainerGenerator, RelativeSource={RelativeSource AncestorType=fluent:ComboBox}}"
                                 GroupByAdvanced="{Binding GroupByAdvancedSample}" />
        </ItemsPanelTemplate>
    </fluent:ComboBox.ItemsPanel>

    <fluent:ComboBox.ItemTemplate>
        <DataTemplate DataType="{ x:Type  local:GallerySampleDataItemViewModel}">
            <Border>
                <StackPanel Orientation="Horizontal"
                            HorizontalAlignment="Left">
                    <TextBlock Text="{Binding Path=Text, Mode=OneWay}"
                               FontSize="10"
                               VerticalAlignment="Center" />
                </StackPanel>
            </Border>
        </DataTemplate>
    </fluent:ComboBox.ItemTemplate>
</fluent:ComboBox>
```

The following happens:
1. `IncreaseSizeCommand` changes `Size` to 12
2. `TextBox.Text` is bound to `Size` so you get the `TextChanged` event
3. `TextChanged` triggers `ChangeSizeCommand`
4. `ChangeSizeCommand` gets the old value (10) of `TextBox.Text` and sets `Size` to 10
5. `TextChanged` triggers `ChangeSizeCommand`
6. `ChangeSizeCommand` gets the old value (10) of `TextBox.Text` and sets `Size` to 10
7. No `TextChanged` is triggered

Fluent.Ribbon is versioned according to semver which means that every major version increase contains breaking changes.

To make it simple:
There are no office version specific themes anymore and "Themes/Office2013/Generic.xaml" got moved to "Themes/Generic.xaml". You now have to replace `pack://application:,,,/Fluent;Component/Themes/Office2013/Generic.xaml` with `pack://application:,,,/Fluent;Component/Themes/Generic.xaml`

Are your icons compiled as resource in your application assembly?

The converter which enables you to just say "images/myicon.png" checks if the file exists on disc, if the file is not on disc it just prepends "pack://application:,,,/" and tries to load that image.
As the images have to be sealed when being converted you get an exception if the resource could not be found.

You can always use the full resource syntax if you want to.
For example "pack://application:,,,/Fluent.Ribbon.Showcase;component/Images/GrowFont.png"
If the images would not be sealed you risk getting this issue https://github.com/fluentribbon/Fluent.Ribbon/issues/493

I am not familiar with your understanding of "themes", but basically I would enable to colourise the controls I mentioned above. Thus, we actually need to introduce new Brushes which define the colour of certain parts of controls (e.g. we introduce a SolidColorBrush named `RibbonTabItemBackgroundBrush` which sets the background color of a non-active `RibbonTab`).

For me "theme" equals different styles and templates for controls.

If you want to start your work the starting points would be:
- Colors.xaml (just a reference file which contains all color and brush resources)
- BaseLight.xaml and BaseDark.xaml (base color schemes, in ThemeManager these are called AppTheme)
- Accent.Template.xaml (used as a template to generate the accent resource dictionaries from GeneratorParameters.json)

- BaseLight and BaseDark contain a resource named `Fluent.Ribbon.AppTheme` which is, indirectly, used in various style triggers. This is achieved by first setting the attached property `Fluent:RibbonProperties.AppTheme` to `{DynamicResource Fluent.Ribbon.AppTheme}` and then triggering on `Fluent:RibbonProperties.AppTheme`. Most of these triggers then set some attached property like `Fluent:RibbonProperties.MouseOverForeground` and don't use a special brush in the control style for the mouse over foreground. That way we are able to use different resources based on the current "app theme". I guess you'll need to introduce a few more attached properties, judging from the list you posted above. This "workaround" is need if, for one "app theme" an accent color should be used for something and in the other an "app theme" color should be used.

They are there because Word behaves different when certain keys are pressed and shift is also pressed.

We should keep that special case by checking if modifier for a given gesture is None, key is F10 and shift is pressed. That case should then not show the key tips. As that shortcut is not only for Word but a global shortcut used to open a context menu.

# Strong Naming Considered Harmful : Strong naming bad. Free your bits.

Don't sign your assemblies. They want to be free. Let them live.

- question: `"But I heard it was good..."`
  answer: No.

- question: `But it was like a whole module in the MCSD course I started 5 years ago...`
  answer: No.

- question: `"Wait, signing things and strong naming sounds like a good idea. Convince me."`
  answer: |
    Consider this all too common occurrence:

    - Your application uses an OSS component called FancyLogging and you’re depending on the latest version 2.1.5.
    - You also use FancyServiceBus that depends on FancyLogging version 2.0.7.
    - You might also have a dependency on FancyIoC which in turn depends on a much older version of FancyLogging 2.0.0.

    Assuming that the authors of FancyLogging are following [Semantic Versioning](http://semver.org/), you should be able to happily use the latest version of FancyLogging because there are no semantically breaking changes between it and the versions that FancyServiceBus and FancyIoC were compiled against. 
    If these assemblies are strong named however, you just set yourself up for a whole lot of assembly version conflicts because .Net matches on the entire version number. 
    At this point, you’re going to be spending some quality time with the Fusion Log Viewer.

    Strong naming conflicts are a common issue when your dependencies improve or change rapidly, and you upgrade somewhat often, and especially when upstream dependencies like log4net, IoC containers, and Newtonsoft.Json are also used by your upstream dependencies.

    (This is borrowed from Jeremy Miller's blog. You can see the original post [here](http://jeremydmiller.com/2014/04/28/fubumvc-lessons-learned-strong-naming-woes-and-workarounds/).)

- question: `But the governance committee says we need to sign our assemblies...`
  answer: |
    Oh. Ok then.

      ...

    Wait. No.
    
    *insert reasons and workarounds here*

- question: `"But [cool open source project] doesn't have strong naming and I need it in my enterprise app that I absolutely need to sign..."`
  answer: |
    Don't hassle the developer to sign their project just so you can use it. There are several workarounds that you can use:

    - Use `ILDASM` and `ILASM` to [sign the assemblies after the fact](http://stackoverflow.com/questions/1379954/how-i-do-a-sign-an-assembly-that-has-already-been-built-into-a-dll-specifically).
    - Use Git submodules to fork the project into your project and build it yourself *examples please*
    - *anything else?*

- question: `"But isn't strong naming a security thing?"`
  answer: |
    Absolutely not. To quote MSDN, ["Do not rely on strong names for security. They provide a unique identity only."](http://msdn.microsoft.com/en-us/library/wd40t7ad(v=vs.110).aspx)


taken from: [strongnamingconsideredharmful](https://github.com/strongnamingconsideredharmful/strongnamingconsideredharmful.github.io)


And more...

Strong-named assemblies are only useful in some rare scenarios. More informations about the reason of this decision can be found here:

- [Still Strong-Naming your Assemblies? You do know it’s 2016, right?](https://www.pedrolamas.com/2016/03/01/still-strong-naming-your-assemblies-you-do-know-its-2016-right/)
- [XAML Behaviors UWP Managed 1.1.0](https://www.pedrolamas.com/2016/02/23/xaml-behaviors-uwp-managed-1-1-0/)
- [Strong-Named Assemblies](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/framework/app-domains/strong-named-assemblies)

Theming got a lot better in version 7.0 these things.
It's currently available as a preview version on nuget.

To change the selected foreground when your item is not part of a contextual group you can overwrite the resource `Fluent.Ribbon.Brushes.RibbonTabItem.Selected.Foreground`.
For mouse over foreground you can overwrite `Fluent.Ribbon.Brushes.RibbonTabItem.MouseOver.Foreground`.

When your tab is inside a contextual group you can use the properties `TabItemSelectedMouseOverForeground`, `TabItemMouseOverForeground` and `TabItemSelectedForeground` on the group.

Please have a look at https://github.com/fluentribbon/Fluent.Ribbon/blob/develop/Fluent.Ribbon/Themes/Themes/Theme.Template.xaml for an overview of which brush/color resource are available for you to overwrite.

You will most likely want to overwrite things like `Fluent.Ribbon.Brushes.RibbonTabControl.Background` and `Fluent.Ribbon.Brushes.RibbonTabControl.Content.Background`.

Alt Gr is composed by "Ctrl+Alt" so Ctrl is the whats doing the job here. Alt Gr does not exist on a Keyboard with US Layout, so i guess the right alt key is just alt.
I introduced the blacklist to remove all modifier keys, because every time a modifier key is pressed together with an KeyTip activation key the activation is invalid. 

you could - to fix the problem - check only for left/right Ctrl at this point, but removing a key from the collection does not fix this issue and will maybe introduce other unwanted behaviors on other keyboard layouts. Furthermore i thought the KeyTips may be changed from the outside (e.g. by a dev using fluent ribbon) thats why i introduced the blacklist and am removing the modifier keys (Alt) that are explicitly triggering the KeyTip mode.

i could change the code to ```if (Keyboard.IsKeyPressed(Key.LeftCtrl) || Keyboard.IsKeyPressed(Key.RightCtrl)) return false;``` but i think this way it covers all cases, even if the KeyTip activation keys are changed from outside.

I analyzed this a bit further. Something changed between `v3.6` and `v7`.

**v3.6** has a `Grid` containing both `Part_TitleBar`, `PART_ContentPresenter` and `PART_WindowCommands` - all placed at `Grid.Row="0"`. Thus, the content will indeed place itself at the top.

**v7** has a `DockPanel` for the caption bar and below it there is this `PART_ContentPresenter`. Thus, the content will be placed below the caption bar.

**Is this change by design?**

If you set Icon to a file/resource path the converter creates a new Image object.
If you set Icon to a Path object the converter essentially does nothing and just returns that object as it is. As Path is a FrameworkElement it can only have one parent. When using the same Path object in multiple places the last user/consumer of that object gets the parent and this causes your Path object only to be visible in one place.
If i extend the converter to convert Path/Shape objects to a DrawingImage, or something like that, it should be possible to display it in multiple places.

There is also more logic inside the converter to return frozen instances of images to enable reuse and also logic to extract images in the desired size from multi-frame images.

These are the things i noticed so far:
- We'd need the new icon size you already mentioned
- I guess the current triggers for the sizes would need to be context aware as in aware of the current mode for the ribbon "full" or "simplified" as the controls in outlook are 
- The new panel control would have to have an overflow button/area. We could copy the overflow logic from the quick access control for this.
- If a group gets collapsed it's moved to the overflow panel and it's children become regular menu items. I have no idea how we should implement this. It wouldn't be a problem for button like controls that have a command, but if people rely on the click event it might get difficult/impossible. But the same, regarding click etc. already applies to the quick access items.
- There seems to be a new group like concept (just have a look at the quick steps "group". It's like a group with some kind of direct menu items. I'd consider this a new type of control or maybe we could solve this by using a Gallery with menu items.
- TextBox like controls would need an watermark. We could copy the code from MahApps.Metro for this or move the code from MahApps.Metro to ControlzEx so it could be shared. Styling would have to be done on our side either way.
- In Outlook the items displayed in the full vs simplified ribbon are not the same. We could solve this by adding flags like "VisibileInSimplifiedView" and "VisibleInFullView" to each control.
- Add a way to switch between the full and the simplified view if switching should be allowed (should also be a new flag somewhere) by the app developer.

The Style for MenuItem was previously, by accident, overwritten by Fluent.Ribbon.
That got fixed and now only the Style for Fluent:MenuItem is set by Fluent.Ribbon.
So what you are observing is because the default WPF style for MenuItem does not convert your PackUri to a proper icon/image.
What you are looking for is the `ObjectToImageConverter` from Fluent.Ribbon which takes care of converting PackUri etc. to an Image object.

What would you think about the following usage?
```
<MenuItem Header="System.Windows.Controls.MenuItem" Icon="{fluent:ObjectToImageConverter 'pack://application:,,,/RibbonIssue;component/Images/Tools/NavForward.png'}"/>
<MenuItem Header="System.Windows.Controls.MenuItem" Icon="{fluent:ObjectToImageConverter 'pack://application:,,,/RibbonIssue;component/Images/Tools/NavForward.png', '16,16'}"/>
<MenuItem Header="System.Windows.Controls.MenuItem" Icon="{fluent:ObjectToImageConverter 'pack://application:,,,/RibbonIssue;component/Images/Tools/NavForward.png', '16,16', {Binding RelativeSource={RelativeSource Self}}}"/>
```

Explanation for the lines:
1. Just take the icon and use it in it's present size
2. Try to make the icon 16x16
3. Try to make the icon 16x16 but take the DPI of the target object into account when trying to extract the icon

Making this possible would only require minimal changes to the converter i mentioned and i would include that in version 7.0 if it helps you.

@soumyanayankar That does not work because the `ItemTemplate` is being used for the right hand content area, in this case.
So you have to use an `ItemContainerStyle` or `ItemContainerStyleSelector` which should be inherited from `BackstageTabControlItemContainerStyleSelector` (otherwise you loose separator styling etc.).

In the style you return from the selector you can then set the content of the tab item to your liking.

The reason for all this is that the `BackstageTabControl` behaves more like a `TabControl` than an `ItemsControl` like `ListBox` for example. And the fact that the method `IsItemItsOwnContainerOverride` only works the way you want if you provide real controls instead of viewmodels.

Your last option might be to just ignore those things, inherit from `BackstageTabControl` and override things like `GetContainerForItemOverride` etc.

The issue with using `IsSelected` as the driver for tab selection is that, before selecting a new tab, the ribbon de-selects the previous one. In addition to that you now have multiple potential sources for the selected tab item as your property also binds two-way. As soon as the ribbon says one tab got de-selected or selected your converter triggers multiple times, thus potentially changing the value back and forth.
This causes your binding value to "flipper" around.

A better approach would be to use the selection properties like `SelectedTabItem` or `SelectedTabIndex` from `Ribbon`. That way you got one binding point instead of multiple.

Looking up resources at the application level is nothing special to Fluent.Ribbon.
It's simply one step in the default resource lookup of WPF.
You can, of course, include the resources at the window level, but you shouldn't do that as it causes performance issues as resources included at the window level have to be loaded every time your show your window.

Fluent.Ribbon has no special code for looking up resources and relies entirely on the way WPF works.
When looking for resources WPF looks at the closest scope first and they works it's way up to the application level.

I don't consider the way you are doing it, in code behind, as hacky. That's the way you should do it if you own the application and care about performance and memory consumption.
It's exactly the same way i use at work where the host application is written in VB6 and parts of the UI are written in WPF.
The only difference is that i use
```
var source = new Uri("........");
var rd = (ResourceDictionary)Application.LoadComponent(source);
Application.Current.Resources.MergedDictionaries.Add(rd);
```

`ElementName` only works if the element has been loaded.
What you could try is to use `TabControlEx` from `ControlzEx` and select every tab in your tabcontrol once when your UI is loaded and set the selection back to the initial tab afterwards.
`TabControlEx` keeps the visual tree of every tab in memory once it has been selected. The regular `TabControl` only keeps the currently selected tabs content in memory and unloads the content from unselected tabs.

What I've found is that, when one uses Fluent.Ribbon and MahApps (which share the same theming), the MetroWindow and the RibbonWindow have different title bar colors. In the case of MetroWindow (MahAapps) it's the Accent color (``"MahApps.Colors.Accent": "#CCxxxxxx"``), on the other hand Fluent.Ribbon uses the AccentBaseColor (``"Fluent.Ribbon.Colors.AccentBaseColor": "#FFxxxxxx"``). I believe that the hover effect is to be achieved by using a color, darker then the current one (AccentBaseColor). Having in mind theming, I suggest transition of color from Fluent.Ribbon.Colors.AccentColor80 to Fluent.Ribbon.Colors.AccentBaseColor. And, of course, RibbonWindow should use AccentColor80 as a title bar background in colorful themes. Another issue related to that one, is that if one uses both libraries together, particularly with the colorful theme of Fluent.Ribbon, and has child windows inherited from MetroWindow (MahApps), he will end up with windows that have different title bar colors. Recently I had such an issue and I fixed it just by setting MahApps's MetroWindow title bar background to the AccentBase (in my case I have generated my own custom color themes for both libraries with the same parameters). Some years ago i wrote a [RegionAdapter](https://github.com/phirSOFT/FluentPrismAdapters) for prism, that kind of did that.

A potential problem with that solution for your case will be thread identity. My code had the assumptions only one ribbon will be shown and there is just one window. The basic idea is to synchronize to insert the items of the child ribbon into the main ribbon and dont't show the child ribbon. When the child ribbon is detached, you remove the items from the main window, and display the child window.

The merging of the two ribbons did work back then, but i never tried to show the child ribbon, so there could be some difficultues.

I don't think that thread identity would be much of a problem (I think it would be safe to say, that ribbon merging across threads is simply not supported). 
I made a prototype earlier this day for my application that looks for a ribbon on a user control / page / whatever and removes it from its parent (content control / panel) and stores the parent reference in an attached property. After that, I can move the items / merge subitems from the source ribbon to the main (target) ribbon (and remembering the source-ribbon and the target list on the ribbon). When I detach it from the main ribbon, I just read the list of attached controls from the ribbon, match the source ribbon and remove all items from the (remembered) parent.
I could also remember if the source ribbon is already merged to another ribbon, so you can't merge the same source ribbon to multiple target ribbons.
I personally think it doesn't make a lot of sense to merge the same ribbon to multiple ribbons as well as showing both the source and the target ribbon at the same time (would defeat the purpose of merging).

Having a class handler clearing all bindings on unload is a very bad idea.

Ok, it's a bug in WPF itself.
If you add `Loaded="FrameworkElement_OnLoaded"` to the `ListBox` the behavior is the same.

This might also be interesting for your memory leak workaround.
If you don't have a loaded handler your unloaded class event handler won't be called.

Interesting conclusion...!

Do I understand correctly the following implications:
 * The unloaded routed event is only being raised for controls which have a non-null loaded event? (Or, at least, only being raised in some circumstances). And this is the WPF bug?
 * Internally, Fluent Gallery probably sets a loaded event handler

Not every control needs the loaded handler.
It depends on the tree and who in that tree has a loaded handler.

In this case no one in the tree for the ListBox has a loaded handler, so the unloaded class event is not fired for anyone when closing the popup.

The gallery on the other hand has a loaded handler, so the unloaded class event is fired for every control that's more up in the tree. So you get events for the gallery, some borders, some decorators and the popup.

The above would also be true if someone directly handled the unloaded event and it does only not work when using a class event handler.

The "offending" line is https://referencesource.microsoft.com/#PresentationFramework/src/Framework/System/Windows/BroadcastEventHelper.cs,332 and the same in line https://referencesource.microsoft.com/#PresentationFramework/src/Framework/System/Windows/BroadcastEventHelper.cs,393

I am not sure if everyone would calls this a bug in WPF.
I would as it's more than surprising and very unexpected. I wasn't aware of this restriction for class event handlers.

@batzen 
Thanks for your review.

**About iconImageBorder:**
I will look into your suggestion about IconBorder (border as icon).

**About separate templates:**
If we talk only about ComboBox, I added Border not for mouseover handling, but for Padding handling.
To make it easier to compare the differences in the ComboBox templates, I added the commit 58f65f9 that matches the order of the properties. Please check it.

Overall I separated the templates for a several reasons.

- Compatibility with existing behaviors
- Avoidance of merge conflicts
- Increasing complexity of triggers

The first is to avoid affecting the existing behavior (classic ribbon). I wanted to avoid adding functionality to the Simple Ribbon that would affect the Classic Ribbon's functionality.

The second is to avoid conflicts. During the implementation of the Simple Ribbon, bug fixes and feature improvements to Fluent.Ribbon continued. If a single template is used to deal with the problem, it is difficult to understand the differences when merging, and conflicts are more likely to occur.

Third, the complexity of triggers is increasing. If we use a single template, IsSimplified will be added to the trigger condition, making it a multi-condition instead of a single condition. I thought this might be a complication.

However, if you think the above reason is not a big deal, I can integrate the template.

@kezara
After some investigation i think it might be a bug in WPF or Windows as the Popup partially receives different DPI information than it should and that seems to be caused if the secondary window has it's X position at the exact edge of the first monitor.
Using `SecondaryStartLocation = SystemParameters.PrimaryScreenWidth + 1;` in your code prevents that issue.

After some more investigation it's really caused by a bug in WPF/Windows.
You can either use the workaround i posted above or you can declare your application as per monitor DPI aware.
The bug in WPF/Windows only happens if your application is not declared as per monitor DPI aware.

I am still very surprised that this is not done by the default WPF application template...

To declare your application as per monitor DPI aware add `<ApplicationManifest>app.manifest</ApplicationManifest>` to any property group in your csproj file.
The content of the `app.manifest` should be something like
```

    <trustInfo xmlns="urn:schemas-microsoft-com:asm.v2">
        <security>
            <requestedPrivileges xmlns="urn:schemas-microsoft-com:asm.v3">

            </requestedPrivileges>
        </security>
    </trustInfo>

    <compatibility xmlns="urn:schemas-microsoft-com:compatibility.v1">

Setting `Size` will only work temporarily if the control is placed in a `RibbonGroupBox` as it interferes with automatic sizing.

If you want to force a certain size you have to set `SizeDefinition="Middle"` (for example) or `SizeDefinition="Middle,Small"` if you only want to prevent your control from being large.

The reason for this is that during measures of `RibbonGroupBox` sizes of controls have to be adjusted and as there is no way to know for sure if `Size` was set because of automatic sizing or was set manually the size is simply overwritten.

It worked more often in versions prior to 10.1, but essentially it was a bug that got fixed in 10.1 by being more consistent when measuring/sizing.

Hi there.
If you want to skip generation of `ContentPresenter` you have to use `UseItemContainerTemplate="true"`.
The following code solves your issue:
```
<Fluent:DropDownButton.Resources>
    <ItemContainerTemplate x:Key="{ItemContainerTemplateKey {x:Type viewModels:MenuItemViewModel}}">
        <Fluent:MenuItem Header="{Binding Header}" 
                         IsCheckable="{Binding IsCheckable}"
                         IsChecked="{Binding IsChecked}"
                         ItemsSource="{Binding Children}"
                         UsesItemContainerTemplate="True" />
    </ItemContainerTemplate>
</Fluent:DropDownButton.Resources>
```

Please do not use `DataType` on the `ItemContainerTemplate`. The generation of that is somewhat broken in WPF itself.

I agree that it would be a bit easier if one could simply use `ItemTemplate`, in combination with `UsesItemContainerTemplate` of course.
Will add that way in the next version.

That's not a bug in Fluent.Ribbon.
You can reproduce the issue without using Fluent.Ribbon.
Use the following code to trigger theme changes and adjust the code in `IconThemeChangeHandler` to also handle `Button` (from WPF)
```
<Expander Header="{DynamicResource Fluent.Ribbon.Images.DefaultPlaceholder}">
    <Button Content="Crash on click" addLogicalChildRepro:ThemesManager.ApplicationThemeChangeHandler="{StaticResource iconThemeChangeHandler}" Click="ButtonBase_OnClick" />
</Expander>
```

The issue here is:
- Setting `ApplicationCurrentTheme` value on `Window` triggers a logical tree walk
- Tree walk hits the `Expander` (or `RibbonGroupBox`) and sets `IsLogicalChildrenIterationInProgress` to `true`
- Our button is part of the logical tree, get's hit by the tree walk and triggers `OnThemeChanged`
- Resources get changed and another tree walk starts (this shouldn't even be possible, IMHO as it destroys the correct values for `IsLogicalChildrenIterationInProgress` of the previous iteration)
- Tree walk hits the `Expander` (or `RibbonGroupBox`) and tries to change a resource reference on it which influences the logical children of it, but in fact WPF is still handling the previous tree walk and `IsLogicalChildrenIterationInProgress` is still `true`

To prevent this you can either place your theme change button somewhere where it doesn't cause such reentrancy issues, or delay the code to change resources via Dispatcher.BeginInvoke.

AI analysis says that even if resources are lazy loaded, static resources inside them are resolved during startup.

```
The deferred content mechanism IS working — values are NOT being instantiated. But the bottleneck is not where you'd expect. Here's the breakdown:

  Where the 87ms goes

  87ms  set_Source
  ├── 80ms  BAML Loading (TransformNodes)
  │   ├── 49ms  SetKeys()                        ← 56% of total!
  │   │   └── 46ms  SetOptimizedStaticResources() ← THE BOTTLENECK
  │   │       └── 46ms  StaticResourceExtension.FindResourceInEnviroment()
  │   │           ├── 21ms  GetAllAmbientValues()
  │   │           │   └── 12ms  LOCK CONTENTION (kernel thread wait!)
  │   │           ├── 12ms  JIT_NewArr1 (array allocations)
  │   │           ├── 9ms   FindAmbientValues()
  │   │           ├── 5ms   GetMember() (XAML type metadata)
  │   │           └── 3.9ms Contains() (dictionary lookups)
  │   ├── 11ms  Baml2006Reader.Read() (reading BAML records)
  │   ├── 6.5ms SetDeferrableContent() (reading key table)
  │   └── 3ms   Hashtable.Insert
  └── 2.5ms  GetResponseStream (fetching the .baml from assembly)

  The real problem: OptimizedStaticResource resolution during key loading

  Even though values are deferred, the BAML key section contains OptimizedStaticResource entries. These are StaticResource references that appear within the key records. From the source code we saw earlier in
  SetKeys:

  for (int i = 0; i < keyCollection.Count; i++)
  {
      KeyRecord keyRecord = keyCollection[i];
      // ...
      if (keyRecord.HasStaticResources)
          SetOptimizedStaticResources(keyRecord.StaticResources, ...);  // ← 46ms HERE
      _baseDictionary.Add(value, keyRecord);
  }

  For every OptimizedStaticResource, SetOptimizedStaticResources calls StaticResourceExtension.TryProvideValueImpl() which tries to resolve the resource immediately by walking up the entire XAML ambient value
  chain. This is a full graph walk, not a simple dictionary lookup.

  Three compounding issues
  Cost: 12ms
  Cause: Lock contention — RtlpEnterCriticalSectionContended → NtWaitForAlertByThreadId. Another thread (likely JIT compiler) holds a CLR critical section, and your UI thread blocks waiting for it. This is pure

    thread scheduling overhead.
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  Cost: 12ms
  Cause: Array allocations — JIT_NewArr1 is called per-lookup inside GetAllAmbientValues. Each StaticResource resolution allocates arrays to collect ambient values. With hundreds of resources, this is heavy GC
    pressure.
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  Cost: 22ms
  Cause: Ambient value walking — FindAmbientValues + GetAllAmbientValues walk the XamlObjectWriter context stack frame by frame, checking each frame's ambient properties. Your ControlzEx theme dictionary likely

    has many cross-referencing resources (brushes referencing colors, styles referencing brushes, etc.), each triggering this walk.
  Why ControlzEx theme dictionaries are especially susceptible

  This is a ControlzEx/MahApps theme dictionary — these tend to have hundreds of resources with heavy StaticResource cross-references (e.g., SomeBrush references SomeColor, SomeStyle references SomeBrush,
  etc.). Each cross-reference inside the deferred key section triggers a full ambient resolution.

  What you can do about it

  1. Split the dictionary — Break the large theme dictionary into smaller MergedDictionaries. Resources referencing each other should live in the same sub-dictionary to reduce ambient walk depth.
  2. Replace StaticResource with DynamicResource where feasible — DynamicResource references are NOT resolved during SetKeys. They're deferred until the resource is actually used. This directly avoids the
  SetOptimizedStaticResources path.
  3. Move loading off the critical path — If this is happening at startup, load the theme dictionary earlier on a background thread (if the dictionary doesn't need to be attached to the visual tree
  immediately), or defer it past the first render.
  4. The 12ms lock contention is a JIT warmup artifact — if this is a cold-start measurement, it will be smaller on subsequent loads. Consider using ReadyToRun (R2R) compilation for the assembly containing the
  theme XAML to reduce JIT pressure.
```

The issue here is that the window behaviors (custom chrome + glow windows) are attached to the window when the window gets initialized (`OnSourceInitialized`).
`WindowChromeBehavior` gets attached first and has to force a redraw of the window as soon as the custom chrome is applied.
That forced redraw call causes the loaded event to be fired.
You close the window when handling the event.
When the `GlowWindowBehavior` is being attached the window already got marked as disposed, without any way to check from the "outside" as there is no public API for that.

The solution to your problem is quite easy.
Just replace your call `this.Close();` with `this.Dispatcher.BeginInvoke(new Action(this.Close));`.
Thank you very much, using `await Dispatcher.InvokeAsync(Close);` indeed avoids the crash.

I know this is somewhat like Chinese whispers. But I let Copilot investigate further to get the correct root cause. But it seems this ticket should be routet to the ControlzEx development:

Thank you for the clarification — you are correct that Fluent.Ribbon itself does not set IsFocusScope since version 3, so the root cause is not there.

After further investigation we now believe the issue is caused by ControlzEx's WindowChrome implementation, specifically its HwndSource message hook handling of WM_ACTIVATE.

**Steps to reproduce:**
1.	Open a modal WPF dialog via ShowDialog() with a RibbonWindow as owner
2.	Close the dialog (e.g. via Cancel / Escape)
3.	Press any key → no keyboard input is processed
4.	Press Tab or click any focusable control → keyboard input works again

**Observed:** After the dialog closes, _IsKeyboardFocusWithin_ is false on the RibbonWindow. _OnPreviewKeyDown_ no longer fires.

**Root cause hypothesis:** WPF's own focus-restore path in _HwndSource.OnMessage_ relies on receiving _WM_ACTIVATE (WA_ACTIVE / WA_CLICKACTIVE)_ with _handled = false_ in order to execute its internal __restoreFocusMode_ logic and call _Keyboard.Focus_ on the previously focused element. ControlzEx registers its _HwndSource_ hook in the _RibbonWindow_ constructor (before _OnSourceInitialized_), and Windows processes hooks in LIFO order. If ControlzEx's hook marks _WM_ACTIVATE_ as handled before WPF's own _HwndSource_ dispatcher processes it, WPF's focus-restore never runs — leaving no element with keyboard focus.

Workaround on application level:

```
protected override void OnActivated(EventArgs e)
{
    base.OnActivated(e);
    if (!IsKeyboardFocusWithin)
        MoveFocus(new TraversalRequest(FocusNavigationDirection.First));
}
```
This works reliably, but it is a compensation for a missing focus-restore that should happen automatically. We would appreciate it if this could be confirmed or ruled out on the ControlzEx side.
